beginner: Economic growth nearly stopped in late 2025, with the economy expanding at only 0.7% instead of the expected 4.4%, mostly because government shutdowns disrupted business.
Inflation is still stubbornly above where the Federal Reserve wants it, with core prices rising 3.1% year-over-year in January.
The Fed will probably cut interest rates only once in 2026 because inflation refuses to fall fast enough, meaning borrowing will stay expensive.
moderate: GDP collapsed to 0.7% annualized growth in Q4 2025 from 4.3% in Q3, a historically sharp reversal driven entirely by government shutdown disruptions that artificially suppressed activity.

Core PCE inflation at 3.1% year-over-year in January remains 110 basis points above the Fed's 2% target, while headline CPI softened to 2.5%, suggesting goods disinflation is masking persistent services price pressures.

The Fed's hawkish pivot to a single 2026 rate cut reflects confidence that growth will recover modestly but signals policymakers see little room for aggressive easing before inflation genuinely retreats to target.
expert: Q4 GDP revised down to 0.7% annualized (from 4.4% preliminary) represents a 370 basis point miss from consensus, with government shutdown effects accounting for the entire quarterly swing and signaling Q1 2026 will likely show a sharp rebound once base effects normalize.

Core PCE at 3.1% in January and core CPI at 2.5% in February create a curious divergence, with PCE's stickiness in services inflation (particularly shelter and health) suggesting the Fed's confidence in a single 2026 cut assumes faster pass-through of energy disinflation and potential demand softening.

Unemployment holding at 4.4% in February despite growth stalling implies either labor demand remains robust or recent weakness is perceived as temporary, a signal the Fed will monitor closely as it calibrates toward a 3.25% year-end terminal rate and risks asymmetric upside surprises if growth resurges faster than expected.

beginner: Canada's economy is being shaken by the Middle East conflict, which is driving up oil prices and creating uncertainty about what will happen next with trade and jobs.
The Bank of Canada is waiting to see new jobs and trade data this week to decide whether it needs to adjust its interest rate strategy amid global turmoil.
With unemployment at 6.74% and inflation under control at 2.29%, Canada has room to cut rates if the economy slows, but geopolitical risks make forecasting harder right now.
moderate: Canada's balance of trade and February unemployment data release this week arrives amid Middle East geopolitical shock, with oil price volatility directly impacting both export revenues and the transmission of energy inflation to broader price measures.

The Bank of Canada currently sits at 2.25%, having already cut significantly, but faces competing signals: unemployment at 6.74% suggests labor market slack, while CPI at 2.29% is already near the 2% target, creating little urgency for immediate action.

Trade dynamics with the US remain the economy's critical wildcard, and oil price swings tied to Middle East escalation could either boost export competitiveness or create demand destruction depending on which direction energy prices move.
expert: Canada's February unemployment and January trade balance data releases this week will test the Bank of Canada's patience with its 2.25% policy rate, as energy price shocks from Middle East conflicts create competing inflationary and demand-destruction channels that make the near-term direction of slack uncertain.

At 6.74% unemployment and 2.29% core CPI, the BoC faces a labor market roughly 40 basis points looser than forecast while inflation sits perfectly at target, but energy volatility could swing both metrics sharply depending on conflict escalation or resolution.

Full-year 2026 growth forecast of 1.7% assumes stable energy prices and US trade stability; a sustained oil price spike above $100 would likely force the BoC to hold at 2.25% longer than markets currently price in, while a collapse below $70 would accelerate rate cuts despite weak growth.

beginner: The UK's trade deficit hit a record $338 billion in 2025 because the country imports far more goods than it exports, though strong services exports like finance and insurance helped soften the blow.
Consumer confidence dropped sharply to 46.0 from 49.0 as people worry about the economy and global uncertainty, which could cause them to spend less money.
The UK releases January GDP data this week while its unemployment sits at 5.2% and inflation at 3.18%, both slightly above where the Bank of England wants them to be.
moderate: The UK's goods trade deficit exploded to a record $338 billion in 2025, but this headline hides a more complex picture: services exports hit a record $261.3 billion, indicating the UK's competitive advantage lies in financial and professional services rather than manufacturing.

Consumer sentiment collapsed to 46.0 from 49.0 amid broader economic anxiety, a signal that comes as CPI at 3.18% remains stubbornly above the Bank of England's 2% target and unemployment at 5.2% offers little cushion to absorb demand shocks.

The Bank of England holds rates at 3.75%, higher than Canada but lower than the US, and January GDP data this week will reveal whether the weak consumer confidence translates into actual spending pullback or remains a lagging psychological indicator.
expert: The UK's goods trade deficit of $338 billion in 2025 represents a structural shift toward services dependency, with record $261.3 billion services surplus reflecting post-Brexit specialization, but this shift leaves the economy vulnerable to financial sector shocks and geopolitical disruptions to service delivery.

Consumer sentiment at 46.0 represents a troubling deterioration that precedes actual spending weakness by 1-2 quarters, and combined with CPI at 3.18% (still 118 basis points above BoE target), suggests the BoE's 3.75% rate may be sufficiently restrictive to generate negative real rates and demand destruction by mid-2026.

January GDP data due this week will likely show modest growth, but forward guidance will focus on whether the BoE can cut toward its 3.25% full-year target without reigniting services inflation; persistent goods trade weakness and consumer caution may force earlier cuts than markets price in if Q1 growth disappoints.

beginner: Japan's economy just grew much faster than expected in the fourth quarter at 1.3% annualized, bouncing back from a painful contraction the quarter before thanks to strong business investment and steady consumer spending.
Japanese workers are earning 3.0% more per year than they did a year ago, a sign that wages are finally rising and the central bank's efforts to warm up the economy are working.

The Bank of Japan is gradually raising interest rates from super-low levels to normalize policy, and with unemployment at just 2.4%, the job market is so tight that businesses have to pay workers more.
moderate: Japan's Q4 2025 GDP came in at 1.3% annualized, a stunning reversal from the prior quarter's -2.3% contraction and crushing the 0.2% consensus, with capital expenditure rising 1.3% quarter-over-quarter signaling businesses finally believe in durable recovery.

Average cash earnings accelerated to 3.0% year-over-year in January, the strongest pace in years, creating a positive feedback loop where wage gains support the Bank of Japan's case for continued gradual rate increases from its current 0.75% level.

Japan's resilience against US trade policy uncertainty and domestic energy price shocks reflects both the economy's structural shift toward investment-led growth and favorable demographics in the labor market, where 2.4% unemployment leaves essentially no slack.
expert: Japan's Q4 GDP print of 1.3% annualized represents a 110 basis point beat versus consensus and marks a decisive reversal of the prior -2.3% contraction, with capital expenditure strength (+1.3% QoQ) indicating private sector confidence has shifted despite US trade uncertainty, a directional signal that the BoJ can accelerate normalization beyond current market expectations of 1.25% by year-end.

Cash earnings growth at 3.0% year-over-year in January supports the BoJ's narrative for ongoing rate hikes, as wage growth now exceeds inflation at 1.53%, creating positive real income growth that should sustain consumption even as policy tightens toward neutral in 2026-27.

The full-year forecast of 0.8% growth appears too conservative relative to momentum; if Q1 2026 maintains similar capital expenditure strength and wage acceleration persists, the BoJ may need to accelerate toward 1.5% by mid-year rather than dribbling cuts or holds through December, a policy error that markets currently underprice given Japan's tight labor market and investment tailwinds.

beginner: German factories just got way fewer orders in January, dropping more than expected, which means companies are hesitant to invest and hire.
Fewer German exports are going to China right now, but the US is buying more German goods instead.
Germany's factories are making less stuff than they did before the pandemic, so the economy is struggling to grow.
moderate: Factory orders plummeted 11.1% in January, nearly triple the forecast, driven by a stunning 39.4% collapse in metal fabrication orders that signals manufacturing confidence has cracked badly.
Industrial production across the eurozone fell 1.5% in January with Germany contracting 1.3%, extending a downtrend that has kept output 9% below 2021 levels as demand remains fragile.

The export mix shifted sharply as German shipments to China dropped 13.2% while US sales surged 11.7%, reflecting both weak China demand and strong North American appetite before potential tariff barriers.
expert: January factory orders crashed 11.1% month-over-month with fabricated metals diving 39.4%, signaling manufacturing confidence collapsed faster than the consensus -4.2% decline predicted, pointing toward Q1 output contraction risks.

Eurozone industrial production contracted 1.5% in January with Germany at -1.3%, extending the nine-point deficit versus 2021 levels and tracking well below the 1.2% full-year growth forecast, implying front-loaded weakness.

Exports to China fell 13.2% while US shipments rose 11.7%, suggesting manufacturers are repositioning supply chains ahead of tariff escalation and that demand destruction in Asia is outpacing North American resilience, likely to constrain 2026 growth to well below consensus.

beginner: France's trade deficit got much smaller than expected in January, which means the country is buying less from abroad and selling steady amounts overseas.
French factories started growing again in February for the first time in a while, a sign that businesses are becoming less gloomy about orders.
French consumers are still unhappy and not spending much, even though confidence improved slightly, so the economy faces a weak demand headwind.
moderate: The January trade balance narrowed sharply to -1.8 billion euros, beating the -5.2 billion consensus as imports collapsed while exports held flat, signaling demand destruction domestically but resilience in external markets.

Manufacturing PMI bounced back to 50.1 expansion in February after months in contraction, the first expansion reading in a while, though new export orders continued to decline suggesting momentum remains fragile.

Consumer sentiment edged up to 42.03 from 41.15 but remains deeply depressed relative to historical averages, indicating households are not yet confident enough to drive growth despite the trade improvement.
expert: The January trade balance compressed to -1.8 billion euros versus -5.2 billion consensus as import volumes fell while export flows stabilized, with current account improving to 2.10 billion euros and signaling involuntary fiscal consolidation through demand destruction.

Manufacturing PMI returned to 50.1 expansion in February marking the first print above the 50 threshold in months, yet new export orders continued declining, indicating cyclical floor support without momentum, consistent with 1.4% full-year growth tracking at consensus midpoint.

Consumer sentiment at 42.03 remains deeply depressed and structurally below pre-pandemic levels, suggesting domestic demand will remain a persistent drag on growth, while the trade improvement reflects import collapse rather than export strength, limiting upside from external rebalancing.

beginner: Italy's short-term borrowing costs jumped higher in a bond auction, showing banks are worried about inflation right now, but long-term costs fell because people trust Italy's finances over many years.
Italian factories expanded in February with confidence at the highest level in many years, suggesting businesses are feeling more optimistic about orders ahead.
Prices for raw materials and goods jumped slightly month-to-month in January but are still falling compared to last year, which is helpful for the economy.
moderate: Three-year BTP yields spiked to 2.75% from 2.36% at auction while 15-year yields fell to 3.85%, creating a rare curve inversion that reveals near-term inflation anxiety offset by longer-term confidence in Italy's fiscal trajectory and eurozone stability.

Manufacturing PMI expanded to 50.6 in February with optimism at multi-year highs, marking a clear inflection from contraction and suggesting Italian manufacturers are positioning for stronger demand despite eurozone-wide headwinds.

January PPI rose 1.5% month-over-month yet remained deflationary at -1.6% year-over-year, indicating input cost pressures are emerging month-to-month but the year-over-year comparison remains benign for manufacturing margins.
expert: Three-year BTP yields jumped 39 basis points to 2.75% while 15-year yields compressed to 3.85%, inverting the curve and signaling market expectations for near-term price pressure contradicting longer-term fiscal confidence, creating tactical positioning risk at the short end.

Manufacturing PMI expanded to 50.6 in February with optimism reaching multi-year highs, a sharp inflection from prior contraction that tracks ahead of the 1% full-year growth consensus and suggests Italian manufacturers see demand window before tariff escalation.

PPI rose 1.5% month-over-month while contracting 1.6% year-over-year, indicating emerging input cost pressures that could compress margins if not passed through, and the combination of rising near-term yields and manufacturing optimism points toward front-loading of orders and inventory builds ahead of external tariff barriers.

beginner: China's exports shot up way faster than expected in February because companies are rushing to ship goods before the US puts higher taxes on them.
China's banks lent out more money in February than expected, and the money supply stayed steady, giving businesses and people more cash to spend.
China is planning its next five-year roadmap at a big government meeting in March, which will set the direction for the economy until 2030.
moderate: The February trade surplus exploded to a record 213.6 billion dollars with exports surging 21.8% year-over-year versus 7.1% consensus, driven by manufacturers front-loading shipments ahead of anticipated US tariff escalations rather than underlying demand strength.

February credit data beat expectations across the board with new yuan loans at 900 billion yuan and total social financing at 2,380 billion yuan, while M2 money supply held steady at 9.0%, indicating policy support is reaching the real economy despite headline economic softness.

China formalizes its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) at the March National People's Congress, marking a critical juncture for long-term growth targets and policy direction that will shape infrastructure investment and industrial priorities for the next lustrum.
expert: February trade surplus hit a record 213.6 billion dollars with exports rocketing 21.8% year-over-year (versus 7.1% consensus), almost entirely driven by pre-tariff front-loading behavior rather than demand recovery, signaling March and Q2 export deceleration as inventory normalization occurs.

February credit aggregates beat with new yuan loans at 900 billion yuan and TSF at 2,380 billion yuan while M2 held at 9.0% growth, indicating monetary accommodation is sustaining credit creation despite weakness in underlying activity, supporting the 4.7% full-year growth target through policy inertia.

Formalization of the 15th Five-Year Plan at the March National People's Congress will reveal whether Beijing is anchoring growth targets at current 4.7% consensus levels or adjusting downward to reflect tariff drag, with the credit and export data suggesting authorities are front-running external demand destruction through domestic credit expansion and export acceleration.

beginner: Oil prices are rising around the world, which pushes up the cost of things Indians buy at the grocery store and gas pump.
India just made a big trade deal with the EU, which means Indian companies can sell more goods to Europe without as many taxes.
India's economy is expected to grow around 7.5 to 7.8 percent this year, making it one of the fastest-growing major economies.
moderate: Oil price increases are creating imported inflation that the Reserve Bank of India cannot fully control without risking a currency crisis, even though headline CPI printed just 1.33% in December, suggesting core price pressures remain elevated beneath the surface.

India sealed a landmark free trade agreement with the EU covering two billion people, the world's largest such zone, which should accelerate goods exports and offset some of the drag from rising import costs.
The government expects 7.5-7.8% growth in fiscal year 2025-26 alongside trade deals with the US, UK, and EU, positioning India to leverage trade partnerships to cushion external price shocks.
expert: India's CPI beat expectations at 1.33% in December, but the RBI flagged this as merely 'the beginning' of inflationary challenges stemming from crude price spikes that imported inflation channels cannot absorb without triggering currency depreciation or policy tightening that would constrain growth toward the 6.3% full-year forecast.

The India-EU free trade deal encompasses two billion people and eliminates tariff barriers, directly supporting the government's push for deals with the US and likely EU completion by year-end, which should improve the current account deficit (forecast at 1.2% of GDP) by expanding merchandise exports.

With the policy rate at 5.25% and real rates potentially turning negative if imported inflation accelerates, the RBI faces a narrow corridor: tightening risks recession in a 7.5-7.8% growth environment, while easing amplifies currency vulnerability as global oil markets remain volatile.

beginner: South Africa's current account (the money flowing in and out of the country) swung from a big deficit to a surplus, which is good news for the rand currency.
The economy grew only 0.4% in the last quarter of 2025, which is very slow and shows that factories, shops, and investment are all struggling.
Manufacturing activity shrank for another month, with the PMI falling to 47.4, signaling that businesses are cutting production and laying off workers.
moderate: South Africa's current account reversed sharply to a 50.2 billion rand surplus in Q4 2025 after a 72 billion rand deficit the quarter before, largely driven by lower import demand as domestic consumption and investment cooled alongside mining output.

GDP expanded just 0.4% annualized in Q4, decelerating from 0.5% in Q3 with year-over-year growth collapsing to 0.8% from 2.1%, signaling that the rebound from load shedding has stalled and demand-side weakness is spreading across sectors.

Manufacturing PMI deteriorated to 47.4 from 48.7, extending contraction in the sector, while the SARB holds rates at 6.75%, leaving limited room to ease if recession risks deepen and unemployment (forecast at 32.5%) stays elevated.
expert: The current account swing to a 50.2 billion rand surplus masks underlying demand collapse: year-over-year growth fell from 2.1% to 0.8% as mining, consumer spending, and capital formation all decelerated, suggesting the surplus reflects import compression rather than export strength, which is unsustainable if recovery requires domestic investment.

Manufacturing PMI at 47.4 signals deepening contraction and potential job losses, contradicting the policy rate hold at 6.75%, which assumes slack can absorb without deflation; if services momentum (up 3.3% year-over-year in January) stalls, the SARB may face stagflation pressures that threaten the 1.5% full-year growth forecast.

South Africa's current account vulnerability to commodity cycles and import sensitivity leaves the economy exposed: surplus conditions now depend on depressed demand, but if oil prices spike further (driven by Middle East disruptions), imported inflation will resurface while growth remains subdued, forcing real rate choices that penalize either employment or currency stability.

beginner: Brazil's inflation ticked up in February to 3.81%, and while that is still below where it was, prices are rising faster month-to-month than expected, showing that price pressure remains.
The central bank has stopped cutting interest rates because oil prices are too high, which means borrowing costs will stay painful for families and businesses.
The services sector, which includes restaurants, shops, and transport, grew a tiny bit in January after shrinking in December, but growth is slowing down overall.
moderate: February CPI landed at 3.81%, down from January's 4.44% but above consensus, while the monthly print of 0.70% exceeded forecasts, signaling that sequential price momentum remains sticky and the central bank's easing cycle may have stopped if crude oil stays elevated.

Banco Central do Brasil lifted the policy rate to 15.0% and signaled the easing window is now shut, trapping real rates at levels that suppress demand and weigh on the 1.7% growth forecast while inflation (expected at 4.2% for the year) remains above the midpoint of the tolerance band.

Services grew just 0.3% month-on-month in January after December contraction, with year-over-year expansion slowing to 3.3%, showing that higher rates are cooling the sectors that had cushioned manufacturing weakness and suggesting unemployment (at 6.78%) could rise if demand keeps softening.
expert: Brazil's February CPI of 3.81% came in above consensus despite a downtrend from 4.44%, with monthly inflation of 0.70% exceeding forecasts and signaling base effects are giving way to persistent price pressures; the central bank's closure of its easing window at a 15.0% policy rate now depends critically on crude stability, as any fresh oil spike would force further tightening into already-fragile growth.

Services momentum collapsed to 3.3% year-over-year in January from higher prints earlier in the cycle, indicating that the demand anchor that cushioned manufacturing weakness is eroding, and with real rates elevated, unemployment (6.78% in February) likely to rise toward the 6.5% full-year forecast as capex and labor demand contract.

Brazil's policy rate at 15.0% prices in a structural inflation premium that reflects currency depreciation risk and fiscal concerns, yet the central bank cannot cut without reigniting pass-through from the weak real if geopolitical oil shocks persist; this leaves real growth exposed below the 1.7% forecast unless commodity prices stabilize or fiscal consolidation restores rate-cut credibility.

beginner: Russia's economy is isolated from most of the world due to sanctions, and oil prices are unstable because of conflict in the Middle East, which hurts Russia's ability to sell energy.
Inflation in Russia is running at 6.01%, higher than most developed countries, which eats into the purchasing power of workers and savers.
The central bank has raised interest rates to 15.5% to fight inflation, but this makes it very expensive to borrow and slows down business and household spending.
moderate: Russia faces geopolitical oil market volatility from Middle East conflict disrupting global flows through the Strait of Hormuz (20% of global oil and LNG normally transit there), which amplifies price swings affecting energy revenues that fund the current account surplus (forecast at 2% of GDP) while international sanctions continue restricting market access.

CPI stands at 6.01% and the central bank has pushed rates to 15.5%, well above the 4.7% inflation forecast for the year, suggesting the bank is pricing in persistent currency depreciation risk and imported inflation pressures from sanctions-driven import constraints.

Unemployment at 2.15% appears tight, but labor market data is unreliable given sanctions disruption and capital controls; the 1.2% growth forecast reflects both isolation from Western markets and the inflationary drag of a weakened ruble that pushes up import prices across the economy.
expert: Russia's 6.01% CPI and 15.5% policy rate reflect a structural inflation regime anchored in ruble depreciation from sanctions, not excess demand, meaning rate hikes contain inflation slowly while suppressing growth below the 1.2% forecast unless oil prices stabilize or sanctions ease.

Middle East conflict has disrupted approximately 20% of global oil and LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz, creating commodity price volatility that directly affects Russia's current account (forecast at 2% of GDP surplus) and constrains monetary policy flexibility, as weaker crude revenues reduce fiscal space while imported inflation persists through the weak ruble.

The divergence between 2.15% unemployment and 15.5% policy rates signals that labor market tightness reflects sanctions-driven supply constraints and capital controls rather than genuine excess demand, meaning the policy rate is a blunt tool that cannot simultaneously defend the currency, control inflation, and support growth, forcing a multi-year adjustment toward lower real output and persistent stagflationary conditions.

beginner.label: Iran War Shuts Oil Highway
beginner.body: The US-Iran war has closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for 20% of global oil. Oil prices hit $100+ per barrel. Energy costs are surging worldwide.

beginner.label: Four Central Banks Meet Today
beginner.body: The Fed, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan, and Bank of England all announce rate decisions today. Markets worry oil shock could force rate hikes instead of cuts.

beginner.label: Global Stocks Drop Hard
beginner.body: Stock markets fell worldwide as inflation fears took hold. The Dow hit a 2026 low. Oil surge threatens economic growth and central bank plans.

moderate.label: Iran War Shuts Oil Highway
moderate.body: Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz since March 4, blocking 20% of global oil supplies. Brent crude jumped from $70 to over $100 per barrel. Only Chinese and Iranian ships pass through. The closure is the worst energy disruption since the 1970s.

moderate.label: Four Central Banks Meet Today
moderate.body: Major central banks announce rates today amid the oil shock. The Fed held rates Wednesday, but markets now price 52% odds the Fed stays on hold all year. The ECB faces rising hike expectations as energy prices threaten inflation targets. Japan's yen weakness adds pressure.

moderate.label: Global Stocks Drop Hard
moderate.body: The Dow fell 768 points to a 2026 low as oil-driven inflation fears gripped markets. European stocks dropped 1.8%, Asian markets fell over 2%. Energy companies gained while other sectors sold off sharply. Bond yields rose on inflation worries.

expert.label: Iran War Shuts Oil Highway
expert.body: Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March 4 has disrupted 8 million barrels per day of oil flow, pushing Brent from $71 to $126 at peak. Only 5 ships transit daily versus 138 pre-war. War risk insurance has spiked, creating a de facto blockade even without formal closure. The US Navy may escort tankers by month-end, but military breakthrough needed to normalize flows.

expert.label: Four Central Banks Meet Today
expert.body: Today marks the first time Fed, ECB, BoJ, and BoE meet simultaneously since December 2021, amid oil shock complexity. Fed held at 3.5-3.75% Wednesday, markets now price 52% odds of no 2026 cuts. ECB faces 42% hike probability on Polymarket, up from 12% pre-war. BoJ may accelerate tightening if USD/JPY breaks 160, triggering carry trade unwind.

expert.label: Global Stocks Drop Hard
expert.body: Global risk-off accelerated with Stoxx 600 down 1.8%, Nikkei -3.4%, Hang Seng -2%. The Dow's 768-point drop marked new 2026 lows as oil-driven stagflation fears emerged. Basic resources led declines on margin squeeze concerns. Financial conditions have tightened since late February, with bond yields and spreads rising alongside equity weakness.
